newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- U.S. retail seen boosting Q1 GDP.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- U.S. retail seen boosting Q1 GDP.

text.p: U.S. economists on Thursday said they revised upward their estimates for first quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth, following sharp revisions in February's U.S. retail sales report.
"A ballpark (GDP) figure now would be 3.25- to 3.5-percent," said Charles Lieberman, managing director and chief economist at Chase Securities Inc.
Lieberman noted his earlier forecast for a 3.1 percent rate of GDP growth in the first quarter also represented an upward revision following last Friday's employment data.
On average, 31 experts in a Reuters poll said first-quarter GDP growth would come in closer to a 3.0 percent annual rate than their previous forecasts for slower growth.
They said the February sales data induced them to increase their GDP estimates another 0.1 to 0.7 percentage point.

Last month's 0.8-percent increase in retail sales slightly exceeded Wall Street expectations. January's revisions were more dramatic, up 1.5 percent from up 0.6 percent, and excluding autos, up 1.4 percent from up 0.4 percent.
As for consumer spending, economists said forecasts, there, too, were being ratcheted upward.
Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist for fixed income at Credit Suisse First Boston, said he was focusing more on the implications for data on February consumer spending.
"Consumer spending could be up in the 6.0- to 7.0-percent range," he said, for perhaps the second time since Alan Greenspan became Federal Reserve chairman.
Data on February personal income and spending will be released on Monday, March 31. In the prior month, incomes rose 0.3 percent, while spending rose 0.7 percent.
Other economists said U.S. trade data for January, slated for release on Thursday, March 20, would affect GDP forecasts.
Without any trade data, projecting GDP is still a bit murky, said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at Nationsbanc Capital Markets Inc.
The international trade balance will be important in determining whether growth rests in the 3.0- to 4.0-percent range, or amounts to something less than 3.0 percent, he said.
"Those are numerical details in a sense because domestic final sales clearly are going to be stronger in the first quarter than they were even in fourth-quarter 1996," he said.
Trade should take some of the sting out of GDP, but inventories would add a little bit back, said Kretzmer.
Despite the strong forecasts for first-quarter GDP, a few analysts said growth will inevitably taper off.
On average, pundits predicted growth rates for the second, third and fourth quarters would decrease to about 2.7, 2.2 and 2.1 percent, respectively.
The slowdown in growth for the subsequent quarters would be a direct result of the Federal Reserve Bank reining in credit, making GDP return toward trend, experts said.

"We would expect with this (retail) news, and with the employment news we had last week, the Fed will raise interest rates," said Kurt Karl, chief economist of WEFA Group's U.S. forercasting center. "That will take a little steam out of the economy," he said.
Full results of the survey follow.
